name: Vanimo
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Ross, Malcolm. 1980. Some elements of Vanimo, a New Guinea tone language. In Boxwell et al. (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 20. Pacific Linguistics A-56:77-109. Canberra: ANU. (PDF via sealang.net PL archive
catalog_quote: Vanimo is a register-tone language (as opposed to a contour-tone language; cf. Ladefoged 1975:227). Pitch-movement is connected mainly with intonation, and only relative syllable-initial pitch is phonemically significant. The 'tones' are describable in terms of the features HIGH and LONG, which my informants feel to be present or absent. One (but never both) of these features may be present, giving three 'tones' (or perhaps two tones and absence of tone) ... [1.4] The suprasegmental systems of Vanimo and English are so diametrically different that an attempt at contrastive description is warranted. English is a stress-timed language with variable word-stress (Ladefoged 1975:222-3). ... Vanimo, however, is a strict syllable-timed language in which most syllables are prominent (some 'toneless' syllables in polysyllabic words and a few monosyllables such as connectives may be non-prominent…

tone_statements.citation: Clifton, John M. 1995. Organised Phonology Data: Vanimo language [VAM], Sandaun Province (Sko Phylum-Level Stock; Vanimo Family). Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics, Papua New Guinea. 4 pp. (SIL-PNG phonology statement; formerly at www-01.sil.org/pacific/png/pubs/928474542501/).
tone_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length): Tone and length are distinctive. There is a three-way contrast between short low, long low, and short falling. Long falling vowels do not occur. Examples: /da/ da 'pig' /dâ/ da' 'west' /daː/ daa 'water' Nasalization is distinctive. In principle, vowels can be nasalized regardless of tone or length. ... There is also considerable support for not representating falling tone. In an attempt to reduce ambiguity for new readers, however, falling tone will be marked in children's books and primers with <'> following the vowel. Adults will rely on context to determine the meaning. Example: /da/ 'pig' is always da; /dâ/ 'west' is da' for children and primers and da for adults.
tone_statements.locator: p.2, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'; p.3, section 'Conventions: Orthographic' (falling-tone marking)
tone_statements.summary: Three-way suprasegmental contrast on the vowel/syllable: short low (unmarked), long low, short falling; long + falling never co-occur (so effectively one marked pitch value, falling/high, versus length, matching Ross's [+HIGH]/[+LONG]/toneless); nasalization cross-classifies freely; no downstep, melodies or stress mentioned; falling tone written <'> after the vowel in primers only.

sources.quote: 'Other members of the family include ... Vanimo/Dumo (Ross 1980) ... To the best of our knowledge (though many Skou languages remain underdocumented), all members of the family are tonal. ... Ross (1980) provides a brief sketch of Dumo, which he describes as having three tones, but the phonetic description of these categories is unclear; he classifies the three using binary features [high] and [long].' No word-stress statement for Dumo; secondary, about a sister language.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2006. Skou Languages. In Keith Brown (ed.), Encyclopedia of Language & Linguistics, 2nd edition. Oxford: Elsevier. DOI 10.1016/B0-08-044854-2/04599-5.
sources.note: Family-level only: Skou languages have three to six tonal contrasts on a monosyllabic word, with the morpheme, not the syllable, as the domain of tone; Vanimo itself is not described.

tone.quote: The languages of the Skou family are spoken along the north coast of New Guinea ... There are 16 known languages in the family ... Tone and in most cases either unusual consonants or a high number of vowels feature prominently. Tonal contrasts range from three to six on a monosyllabic word, but in all well-investigated cases the domain of tone is the morpheme, not the syllable.
